title: Working with Text
intro: Rust's text tools are methods on `str` itself: `trim`, `split`, `split_once`, `replace`, `parse`, `starts_with`, `find`. Most of them hand back views into your text instead of copies.

coming_from.go: The `strings` package becomes methods on `str`: `trim` is `TrimSpace`, `split_once` is `strings.Cut`, `parse` replaces `strconv`. `find` returns an `Option<usize>` instead of -1, and `split` gives a lazy iterator, not a slice.
coming_from.kotlin: These are close to Kotlin's string methods: `trim`, `split`, `replace`, `starts_with`. `find` returns `Option<usize>` instead of -1, and `split` gives a lazy iterator rather than a `List`, so you can't index it.
coming_from.python: `strip` is `trim`, `partition` is `split_once` (which returns an `Option`), and `int(s)` is `s.parse()`. `find` gives `Option<usize>` instead of -1, and `split` is a lazy iterator, not a list.
coming_from.typescript: `trim`, `split` and `startsWith` (`starts_with`) carry over. Rust's `replace` changes every match, where JS's `replace` with a string changes only the first (`replaceAll` is the equal). `parse` returns a `Result` instead of `NaN`, `find` returns an `Option` instead of -1, and `split` is a lazy iterator, not an array.
coming_from.java: `trim`, `split`, `replace` and `starts_with` correspond to Java's `strip` or `trim`, `split`, `replace` and `startsWith`, but most return views into your text instead of new Strings. `split` takes a plain pattern, not a regex, and returns a lazy iterator, so `parts[0]` doesn't work; use `.next()` or `split_once`.
coming_from.csharp: `trim`, `split`, `replace` and `find` match `Trim`, `Split`, `Replace` and `IndexOf`, but `trim` and `split` hand back views instead of new strings. `split` returns a lazy iterator rather than an array, so take pieces with `split_once`, `.next()` or `collect()`.
coming_from.c: Rust's `trim`, `split` and `find` do what you'd build from `isspace`, `memchr` and `strstr`, as methods on `str`. `split` only borrows the text and never writes into it the way `strtok` does, and `parse` returns a `Result` instead of a `strtol` end pointer.
coming_from.cpp: These methods work on `&str` like `std::string_view` functions, and `split` is lazy like `std::views::split`. Rust has `trim` and `split_once` built in, where C++20 has neither. `parse` is closest to `from_chars`, which stops at the first non-digit instead of failing.

notes: `trim`, `split`, `split_once` and friends return `&str` views into the original text. Cutting allocates and copies no text. You get a new `String` only when you ask for one with `.to_string()` or `.to_owned()`.
Methods that have to change the text, like `to_uppercase` and `replace`, return a new `String`. You can tell from the signature: `-> String` means new memory, `-> &str` means a view.
`find` returns `Option<usize>`: `Some(10)` or `None`. Go's `strings.Index`, Java's `indexOf` and Python's `str.find` return -1 instead; here the type makes you handle the missing case.
`"30".parse()` works for any type that implements `FromStr`: numbers, bools, IP addresses, your own types. The type you write on the left (`let age: u32`) picks which one.
`split` is lazy: it finds the next piece only when you ask for it. That's why it can't be indexed like a list. See the gotcha.
To build text in a loop, `push_str` onto one `String`. It grows in place, like a string builder. `format!` makes a new `String` from a format string.
Need regular expressions? They're not in std. The usual choice is the `regex` crate, maintained by the Rust project's regex team. `Regex::new` returns a `Result`.

gotcha.title: Taking the first piece of a split with [0]
gotcha.looks_fine: `strings.Split` gives you a `[]string`, so `parts[0]` is the first piece. Same in Kotlin, Python, Java and the rest.
gotcha.rust_sees: `split` doesn't give you a list. It gives you an iterator that finds pieces one at a time as you ask, and an iterator has no `[0]`.
gotcha.why: Being lazy means `split` allocates nothing until you decide what you need. If you only want the first piece, `.next()` gets it without building a list at all. If you want to index around, `.collect()` into a `Vec<&str>`: that allocates one small list of views, and still copies none of the text.

go.says: Go runs this and prints ana. `strings.Split` builds a whole slice right away, so `[0]` works.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints ana. `split` builds a whole `List` right away, so `[0]` works.

python.says: Python prints ana. `split` builds a whole list right away, so `[0]` works.
python.code:
line = "ana,30,lisbon"
parts = line.split(",")
name = parts[0]
print(name)

typescript.says: Prints ana. `split` returns a real array, so `[0]` gives the first piece.

java.says: `split` returns a plain String array, so `parts[0]` is ana. One surprise: `split` takes a regex, so `split(".")` or `split("|")` won't do what you expect.

csharp.says: `Split` returns a plain string array, so `parts[0]` is ana. Every call builds a new array and new strings for each piece.

c.says: C has no split, so `strtok` is the natural pick, and it writes into the text it splits. Here that text is a string literal in read-only memory, so gcc says nothing and AddressSanitizer reports a SEGV inside `strtok`.

python.code:
line = "  name=Ana, age=30, city=Lisbon  "

clean = line.strip()  # a new str: Python strings never change in place
print(f"[{clean}]")

# split on ',', strip each piece, split once on '='
for field in clean.split(","):
    key, sep, value = field.strip().partition("=")
    if sep:
        print(f"{key:>5} -> {value}")

# text to number: int raises ValueError on bad input
try:
    age = int("30")
except ValueError:
    age = 0
print(f"next year: {age + 1}")

shout = clean.upper().replace(", ", " | ")
print(shout)

print(f"starts with name: {clean.startswith('name')}")
print(f"position of age: {clean.find('age')}")  # -1 when missing

words = ["build", "with", "rust"]
print("-".join(words))

# collect pieces in a list and join once, like strings.Builder
parts = []
for i in range(1, 4):
    parts.append(f"{i};")
print("".join(parts))

	fmt.Printf("Fields(\" a  b\\t\"):    %q\n", strings.Fields(" a  b\t"))
	fmt.Printf("Fields(\"\"):           %q\n", strings.Fields(""))
	fmt.Printf("SplitN(\"k=v=w\", \"=\", 2): %q\n", strings.SplitN("k=v=w", "=", 2))

	before, after, found := strings.Cut("k=v=w", "=")
	fmt.Println("Cut:", before, after, found)
	fmt.Printf("TrimLeft(\"///a\", \"/\"): %q\n", strings.TrimLeft("///a", "/"))

	fmt.Println("Replace(\"a-a-a\", \"-\", \"+\", 1):", strings.Replace("a-a-a", "-", "+", 1))
	fmt.Println("ReplaceAll(\"a-a-a\", \"-\", \"+\"):", strings.ReplaceAll("a-a-a", "-", "+"))
	fmt.Printf("Ext(\".bashrc\"): %q, Ext(\"a.tar.gz\"): %q\n", filepath.Ext(".bashrc"), filepath.Ext("a.tar.gz"))

	for _, text := range []string{"42", "+42", " 42", "1_000", "٣", "3000000000"} {
		n, err := strconv.Atoi(text)
		fmt.Printf("Atoi(%q): %d, %v\n", text, n, err)
	}

	fmt.Println("ToUpper(\"straße\"):", strings.ToUpper("straße"))
	fmt.Println("EqualFold(\"É\", \"é\"):", strings.EqualFold("É", "é"))
}
